hinweis: ORMA auf Englisch (20. Oktober 2026): Einstieg und Spielaufträge der 48 Pilot-Konstellationen, je ID, dieselbe Struktur wie pilot.json; Originaltext und Originalfrage kommen aus src/doppelspalt/src/data/en/ (die Konstellationen von ORNA auf Englisch). Keine Zitate und keine Äusserungen der genannten Personen.

eva-hesse__susan-leigh-star.einstieg: Eva Hesse's works are ageing. This confronts museums with practical decisions: how to conserve, store and exhibit them. Susan Leigh Star studies infrastructures, that is, what provides stability in the background. With Hesse it becomes visible that this care helps determine how a changeable work lives on. The sculpture and its care cannot be fully separated.

auftraege.beispiel: Choose an object near you both. What would someone have to do so that it still exists in twenty years? What would be allowed to change in the process?
auftraege.einwand: Care can also falsify a work. Find a case in which it would be better to let something age rather than preserve it.
auftraege.gestaltung: For an object you both know, write a care instruction in three sentences: one preserves it, one changes it, one leaves open who is responsible.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Choose an object near you. What would someone have to do so that it still exists in twenty years? What would be allowed to change in the process?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Care can also falsify a work. Find a case in which it would be better to let something age rather than preserve it.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: For an object you know well, write a care instruction in three sentences: one preserves it, one changes it, one leaves open who is responsible.

tehching-hsieh__claude-shannon.einstieg: Tehching Hsieh's time-clock performance produces an enormous sequence of clear timestamps. Claude Shannon could treat such distinguishable signs as information that can be transmitted. Yet the stamp contains neither the tiredness nor the missing sleep nor the lost freedom of movement that go into producing it. A precise date can be far removed from the time a body has actually spent.

auftraege.beispiel: Each of you, name a timestamp from your everyday life: a receipt, a message, a photo with a date. What does it know about that moment, and what does it lack?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps it is good that a stamp does not contain the tiredness. Find a case in which it helps that information stays separate from the body.
auftraege.gestaltung: Note the current time on a slip of paper and write beneath it three things this number does not capture. Put the slip somewhere you will both find it again later.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a timestamp from your everyday life: a receipt, a message, a photo with a date. What does it know about that moment, and what does it lack?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps it is good that a stamp does not contain the tiredness. Find a case in which it helps that information stays separate from the body.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Note the current time on a slip of paper and write beneath it three things this number does not capture. Put the slip somewhere you will find it again later.

dan-graham__donna-haraway.einstieg: Dan Graham's mirrors and transparent pavilions offer no view from nowhere. What one sees depends on where a body stands, who is on the other side and what happens to be reflected. Donna Haraway calls this situated knowledge: observation remains valid but is tied to a place. With Graham, one's own standpoint becomes part of the picture.

auftraege.beispiel: Stand side by side in front of a window or a mirror and both describe what you see. Which difference comes only from where you are standing?
auftraege.einwand: Sometimes a view as neutral as possible is needed: for a measurement, in court, on a map. Look for an argument against every view being bound to a position.
auftraege.gestaltung: Draw the same object on paper from two different spots. Give each drawing a title that names the standpoint, not the object.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Stand in front of a window or a mirror and describe what you see. Then take a step to the side: which difference comes only from where you are standing?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Sometimes a view as neutral as possible is needed: for a measurement, in court, on a map. Look for an argument against every view being bound to a position.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Draw the same object on paper from two different spots. Give each drawing a title that names the standpoint, not the object.

felix-gonzalez-torres__judith-butler.einstieg: The works of Felix Gonzalez-Torres continue to exist even though parts of them are taken away, used up and made anew. The work remains recognisable even when its material components change. Judith Butler describes identity in a similar way: not as a fixed core but as something that stays in effect through repeated doing. Identity would then lie in a regulated repetition, not in unchanged substance.

auftraege.beispiel: Name something that has stayed the same for you even though all its parts have changed: a club, a recipe, a ritual. What is repeated so that it stays the same?
auftraege.einwand: Is there a limit? Describe a change after which you would both say: this is no longer the same, even if the rule is still being followed.
auftraege.gestaltung: In one sentence, invent a rule by which a work made of everyday things can be made anew again and again. What has to stay the same, what may change?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name something that has stayed the same for you even though all its parts have changed: a club, a recipe, a ritual. What is repeated so that it stays the same?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Is there a limit? Describe a change after which you would say: this is no longer the same, even if the rule is still being followed.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: In one sentence, invent a rule by which a work made of everyday things can be made anew again and again. What has to stay the same, what may change?

rebecca-horn__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.einstieg: Rebecca Horn connects bodies with machines whose movements can repeat. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun studies habits through which technical orders come to be taken for granted. Horn prevents this taking for granted. Her apparatuses make every repetition palpable, because the body has to relate to them anew each time. What usually goes unnoticed becomes a task here.

auftraege.beispiel: Which device do you each use without thinking about it? Remember the first time, when it was still unfamiliar. What did you notice back then?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps habit is not a loss but a relief. Find a case in which it is good that technology goes unnoticed.
auftraege.gestaltung: Make an everyday hand movement on your phone, such as unlocking or swiping, ten times very slowly. Describe what you notice that otherwise disappears.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Which device do you use without thinking about it? Remember the first time, when it was still unfamiliar. What did you notice back then?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps habit is not a loss but a relief. Find a case in which it is good that technology goes unnoticed.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Make an everyday hand movement on your phone, such as unlocking or swiping, ten times very slowly. Describe what you notice that otherwise disappears.

marina-abramovic__lucy-suchman.einstieg: Marina Abramović often sets only a few rules and leaves much to the actual meeting of bodies. Lucy Suchman understands action as a coordination that only takes shape in the course of a situation. The posture, gaze, waiting and reaction of the audience therefore do not merely accompany the performance from outside. They help change what the action becomes in that moment.

auftraege.beispiel: Remember a situation in which spectators changed something: a concert, a speech, a game. How did you notice that they had become part of the action?
auftraege.einwand: Not every audience is meant to take part. Find an example in which watching is deliberately meant to remain without influence, and say why that might be important.
auftraege.gestaltung: Set a rule for one minute, for example: we look at each other without speaking. Carry it out. What did the other person change that was not in the rule?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Remember a situation in which spectators changed something: a concert, a speech, a game. How did you notice that they had become part of the action?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Not every audience is meant to take part. Find an example in which watching is deliberately meant to remain without influence, and say why that might be important.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Set a rule for one minute, for example: I look out of the window without moving. Carry it out. What did the surroundings change that was not in the rule?

mona-hatoum__hannah-arendt.einstieg: Hannah Arendt compares a shared world to a table: it connects the people gathered around it and separates them at the same time. Mona Hatoum repeatedly turns familiar things and spatial orders into precarious situations. Then a shared object no longer guarantees a shared experience. People can stand in front of the same thing and yet be affected by it quite differently.

auftraege.beispiel: Name a place you both know. Is it equally accessible, equally safe, equally familiar to each of you? What is different for one person than for the other?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps a shared world does not need equal conditions at all. Look for an argument that it is precisely difference that makes a space shared.
auftraege.gestaltung: Place an object on the table between you. Each describe it in one sentence from your own point of view. Then write a third sentence that is true for both of you.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a place you share with others. Is it equally accessible, equally safe, equally familiar to everyone? What is different for you than for others?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps a shared world does not need equal conditions at all. Look for an argument that it is precisely difference that makes a space shared.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Place an object on the table in front of you. Describe it in one sentence from your point of view and in one sentence as a quite different person might see it. Then write a third sentence that is true for both.

louise-bourgeois__henri-bergson.einstieg: Louise Bourgeois returns again and again to earlier experiences, figures and spaces. Henri Bergson does not understand memory as a stored image that is retrieved unchanged. The past acts anew out of each present. Bourgeois's Cells show precisely this movement: a memory takes on a form again, but never the same present.

auftraege.beispiel: Briefly tell each other an early memory you have often told before. What do you tell differently today than you used to?
auftraege.einwand: Some memories are meant precisely not to change: witness statements, minutes, days of remembrance. Find an argument for holding memory fixed.
auftraege.gestaltung: Give a memory a small place: three objects from your surroundings, arranged on a table. What does the arrangement show that the telling does not say?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of an early memory you have often told before. What do you tell differently today than you used to?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some memories are meant precisely not to change: witness statements, minutes, days of remembrance. Find an argument for holding memory fixed.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Give a memory a small place: three objects from your surroundings, arranged on a table. What does the arrangement show that the telling does not say?

on-kawara__elena-esposito.einstieg: On Kawara paints a date only on the day it designates. Elena Esposito studies a future that is expected in the present but cannot be known. Kawara's rule separates these two sides sharply. Tomorrow's date we already know as a possibility. As a painting, however, it can only come into being once the day has actually become present.

auftraege.beispiel: Name a date you already know even though it has not yet arrived. What do you know about it today, and what can only come into being on that day?
auftraege.einwand: Appointments, deadlines and birthdays take effect before they arrive. Show with an example how a future changes the present even though it has not yet occurred.
auftraege.gestaltung: Both of you write today's date on a sheet of paper as carefully as possible. On the back, note what would have to be written on such a sheet tomorrow and what you cannot yet know today.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a date you already know even though it has not yet arrived. What do you know about it today, and what can only come into being on that day?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Appointments, deadlines and birthdays take effect before they arrive. Show with an example how a future changes the present even though it has not yet occurred.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write today's date on a sheet of paper as carefully as possible. On the back, note what would have to be written on such a sheet tomorrow and what you cannot yet know today.

doris-salcedo__jacques-derrida.einstieg: Doris Salcedo gives loss a material trace without making what was lost present again. Jacques Derrida describes the trace as the effect of an absence that does not simply disappear. Salcedo's furniture, cracks and blocked spaces make this tension physically palpable. What is missing is not replaced, but it changes the present in which one encounters it.

auftraege.beispiel: Look in your surroundings for a trace of something that is no longer there: an imprint, a gap, a worn spot. What does it tell about what is missing?
auftraege.einwand: A trace can also cover over an absence, because it puts something tangible in its place. When does a trace console too much?
auftraege.gestaltung: Take an object off the table and leave its place empty. Write a sentence that describes the empty place without naming the object.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Look in your surroundings for a trace of something that is no longer there: an imprint, a gap, a worn spot. What does it tell about what is missing?
auftraege_allein.einwand: A trace can also cover over an absence, because it puts something tangible in its place. When does a trace console too much?
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Take an object off the table and leave its place empty. Write a sentence that describes the empty place without naming the object.

sol-lewitt__george-spencer-brown.einstieg: George Spencer-Brown begins with a distinction: a boundary is drawn, and with it two sides come into being. Sol LeWitt, too, often begins with a stipulation, such as an instruction, a grid or rules for lines. Different executants understand the same instruction differently, and nobody carries out the same plan identically twice. The rule opens up possibilities but does not fully contain its execution.

auftraege.beispiel: Think of a recipe, a rule of a game or a set of directions. Where, in carrying it out, did you deviate from the instruction without breaking it?
auftraege.einwand: If every execution turns out differently, why have a rule at all? Find an argument that the form does lie in the rule after all.
auftraege.gestaltung: Write a drawing instruction in one sentence, for example: draw ten straight lines that do not touch. Both carry it out on paper and compare the results.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a recipe, a rule of a game or a set of directions. Where, in carrying it out, did you deviate from the instruction without breaking it?
auftraege_allein.einwand: If every execution turns out differently, why have a rule at all? Find an argument that the form does lie in the rule after all.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write a drawing instruction in one sentence, for example: draw ten straight lines that do not touch. Carry it out twice on paper and compare the two results.

donald-judd__michel-serres.einstieg: Donald Judd arranges bodies and intervals with great, measurable precision. Michel Serres, by contrast, also thinks space through paths, neighbourhoods and transitions. With Judd, the distance between two objects remains measurably the same, while their relationship changes as one walks. What stands side by side only becomes a sequence of nearness and distance through the path of the body.

auftraege.beispiel: Name two places that lie close together on the map but feel far apart to you, or the other way round. What makes the way longer or shorter?
auftraege.einwand: A metre is a metre. Look for an argument that the measurable distance matters more than the experienced path.
auftraege.gestaltung: Place two objects on the floor one step apart. Walk past them once in a straight line and once in an arc. Describe when they seemed closer to you.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name two places that lie close together on the map but feel far apart to you, or the other way round. What makes the way longer or shorter?
auftraege_allein.einwand: A metre is a metre. Look for an argument that the measurable distance matters more than the experienced path.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Place two objects on the floor one step apart. Walk past them once in a straight line and once in an arc. Describe when they seemed closer to you.

eva-hesse__george-spencer-brown.einstieg: George Spencer-Brown has form begin with a boundary that distinguishes two sides. Eva Hesse's soft, hanging and ageing materials call the stability of such a boundary into question. A contour can sag, lose tension or appear differently because of the material. The form does not necessarily disappear as a result. It shows that a boundary can exist without being unchangeable.

auftraege.beispiel: Look for an object whose outline gives way: a cushion, a jumper over the back of a chair, a bag. Where is its boundary, and how much may it give way?
auftraege.einwand: Some boundaries have to be firm for something to work: a doorstep, a line on a playing field. Find an argument that form needs a stable boundary.
auftraege.gestaltung: Lay a boundary on the table with a piece of string or a cloth. Change it slightly three times without lifting it. At what point is it a different form?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Look for an object whose outline gives way: a cushion, a jumper over the back of a chair, a bag. Where is its boundary, and how much may it give way?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some boundaries have to be firm for something to work: a doorstep, a line on a playing field. Find an argument that form needs a stable boundary.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Lay a boundary on the table with a piece of string or a cloth. Change it slightly three times without lifting it. At what point is it a different form?

tehching-hsieh__lucy-suchman.einstieg: Tehching Hsieh formulates rules that are meant to hold for a whole year. Lucy Suchman shows that a plan can never fully anticipate the concrete action. The longer Hsieh's rule lasts, the more of the unplanned it has to pass through: tiredness, weather, illness, encounters and practical obstacles. The plan stays the same, but its survival depends every day on how it is carried out in the situation.

auftraege.beispiel: Each of you, name a resolution you kept for longer than a month. What did you have to adjust along the way so that it survived?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps a plan is strong precisely when it does not adapt to the situation. Find a case in which rigidity is better than adaptation.
auftraege.gestaltung: Together, write a rule for the next seven days that fits into one sentence. Beneath it, note three situations in which it would be hard to keep.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a resolution you kept for longer than a month. What did you have to adjust along the way so that it survived?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps a plan is strong precisely when it does not adapt to the situation. Find a case in which rigidity is better than adaptation.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write a rule for the next seven days that fits into one sentence. Beneath it, note three situations in which it would be hard to keep.

dan-graham__henri-bergson.einstieg: Dan Graham's video delays divide time into precisely measurable seconds. Henri Bergson distinguishes such measurable time from lived duration. In front of the monitor the two meet. Ten seconds can be fixed with technical exactness, yet the experience of seeing oneself again with a delay does not break down into the same units. The measured delay produces a duration that passes differently from the clock.

auftraege.beispiel: Each of you, name a situation in which ten seconds were very long or very short. What changed the duration?
auftraege.einwand: The clock is the same for everyone, and that is exactly why we can make appointments. Find an argument that measured time matters more than experienced time.
auftraege.gestaltung: Both close your eyes and open them when you think ten seconds have passed. Let a clock run alongside. Who was how far off, and what did you go by?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a situation in which ten seconds were very long or very short. What changed the duration?
auftraege_allein.einwand: The clock is the same for everyone, and that is exactly why we can make appointments. Find an argument that measured time matters more than experienced time.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Close your eyes and open them when you think ten seconds have passed. Let a clock run alongside. How far off were you, and what did you go by?

felix-gonzalez-torres__michel-serres.einstieg: Felix Gonzalez-Torres lets parts of his works leave the exhibition space. Paper is taken away, sweets are eaten, the stocks are replenished later. Michel Serres is interested in transitions and in the fact that a transmission does not bring what is transmitted unchanged from one place to another. With Gonzalez-Torres, this change is part of the work. It does not persist in spite of being passed on, but through it.

auftraege.beispiel: Name something you have passed on or received: a book, a recipe, a joke. What changed along the way, and what remained?
auftraege.einwand: Some things are meant precisely not to be passed on, so that they are preserved: an original, a secret, a place. Find an argument for not letting something circulate.
auftraege.gestaltung: Write a sentence on a slip of paper and pass it back and forth. At each handover, each person may change exactly one word. After six handovers: is it still the same sentence?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name something you have passed on or received: a book, a recipe, a joke. What changed along the way, and what remained?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some things are meant precisely not to be passed on, so that they are preserved: an original, a secret, a place. Find an argument for not letting something circulate.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write a sentence on a slip of paper and copy it out six times. Change exactly one word with each copy. Is the last one still the same sentence?

rebecca-horn__donna-haraway.einstieg: Rebecca Horn connects bodies with feathers, rods, masks and machines. Donna Haraway's figure of the cyborg disrupts the clear boundary between organism and technology. Horn's extensions do not simply illustrate this figure. They let one experience bodily that reach, touch and action belong neither to the body alone nor to the apparatus alone.

auftraege.beispiel: Which aid do you no longer feel as an object at all when using it: a pair of glasses, a pen, a bicycle? Since when has it been part of you?
auftraege.einwand: A tool remains a tool; it can be put down at any time. Look for an argument that the boundary between body and technology stays clear.
auftraege.gestaltung: Extend one arm with an object, such as a spoon or a ruler, and touch three different surfaces with it. Describe where you feel the touch.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Which aid do you no longer feel as an object at all when using it: a pair of glasses, a pen, a bicycle? Since when has it been part of you?
auftraege_allein.einwand: A tool remains a tool; it can be put down at any time. Look for an argument that the boundary between body and technology stays clear.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Extend one arm with an object, such as a spoon or a ruler, and touch three different surfaces with it. Describe where you feel the touch.

marina-abramovic__elena-esposito.einstieg: In many of her works, Marina Abramović announces duration and conditions in advance. Elena Esposito shows that ideas of the future already change the present, even though what is to come has not yet occurred. Whoever knows that a performance will last six hours already experiences the first moment within the horizon of that end. The fixed duration raises expectations without fixing the course.

auftraege.beispiel: Remember something whose end was set from the start: a journey, a course, a visit. How did knowing the end change the beginning?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps an announced end spoils the present, because one does nothing but count. Find an argument for beginnings without a known end.
auftraege.gestaltung: Agree on a minute of silence and say out loud beforehand when it will end. Repeat it without announcement; one person ends it. What was different?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Remember something whose end was set from the start: a journey, a course, a visit. How did knowing the end change the beginning?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps an announced end spoils the present, because one does nothing but count. Find an argument for beginnings without a known end.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Set an alarm for one minute and stay silent until it rings. Repeat it without the alarm and stop when it feels like enough. What was different?

mona-hatoum__judith-butler.einstieg: Judith Butler examines how bodies become recognisable as particular bodies within social norms. Mona Hatoum tips familiar orders over, so that an object or space loses its accustomed legibility. This concerns not only meaning but the body that has to relate to it. Something can look familiar and yet demand a different movement, distance or caution.

auftraege.beispiel: Name a place or object where your body reacts differently than its appearance would lead you to expect: a slippery staircase, a chair that is too low. Which rule of behaviour begins to waver?
auftraege.einwand: Norms help because we do not have to think every situation through afresh. Find an example in which a practised norm protects the body.
auftraege.gestaltung: Use an everyday object differently from how it is intended for five minutes, say a cup with the other hand or a chair the wrong way round. Note what changes in your posture.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a place or object where your body reacts differently than its appearance would lead you to expect: a slippery staircase, a chair that is too low. Which rule of behaviour begins to waver?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Norms help because we do not have to think every situation through afresh. Find an example in which a practised norm protects the body.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Use an everyday object differently from how it is intended for five minutes, say a cup with the other hand or a chair the wrong way round. Note what changes in your posture.

louise-bourgeois__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.einstieg: Louise Bourgeois returns again and again to particular memories and forms. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun studies habits that become stable through repetition. Bourgeois's return, however, differs from a soothing routine. The familiar can produce a new tension with each repetition and precisely in this way remain effective. Repetition holds fast and changes at the same time.

auftraege.beispiel: Name a song, a place or a photo you keep returning to. Was it the same the last time as the first time?
auftraege.einwand: Many rituals work precisely because they always stay the same. Find an argument that repetition protects a memory rather than changing it.
auftraege.gestaltung: Both draw the same object from memory three times in a row, without looking at the previous drawing. Compare: what shifts from one time to the next?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a song, a place or a photo you keep returning to. Was it the same the last time as the first time?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Many rituals work precisely because they always stay the same. Find an argument that repetition protects a memory rather than changing it.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Draw the same object from memory three times in a row, without looking at the previous drawing. Compare: what shifts from one time to the next?

on-kawara__hannah-arendt.einstieg: On Kawara turns a single day into a lasting object. His date painting can only come into being on that one day. Hannah Arendt understands the shared world as something that exists between people and outlasts their lifetimes. Once Kawara's painting is finished, many people can look at this past day at different times. A personal now is given a place in a shared world.

auftraege.beispiel: Name a day that many people remember together, and one that only the two of you know. What makes the one shared and the other private?
auftraege.einwand: A painted date shows only a number, not the day itself. Find an argument that a single day cannot be shared at all.
auftraege.gestaltung: Hold today in an object that will still be there tomorrow: a slip of paper, a stone, a note in a book. What has to be on it for someone else to understand it?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a day that many people remember together, and one that only you know. What makes the one shared and the other private?
auftraege_allein.einwand: A painted date shows only a number, not the day itself. Find an argument that a single day cannot be shared at all.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Hold today in an object that will still be there tomorrow: a slip of paper, a stone, a note in a book. What has to be on it for someone else to understand it?

doris-salcedo__susan-leigh-star.einstieg: Doris Salcedo makes loss visible in furniture, walls and public interventions. Susan Leigh Star asks about the often invisible structures that support a shared practice. Public remembrance, too, needs such conditions. Institutions, places, care and rituals help decide whether a material trace persists and can be sought out again.

auftraege.beispiel: Think of a monument, a memorial plaque or a grave you know. Who makes sure that it remains, and what would happen without this care?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps remembrance needs no infrastructure at all, only people who tell. Find an example of remembrance without a place and without an institution.
auftraege.gestaltung: Choose a memory you both share. Decide where, how often and by whom it is to be recalled over the course of a year. Write this small infrastructure down in three lines.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a monument, a memorial plaque or a grave you know. Who makes sure that it remains, and what would happen without this care?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps remembrance needs no infrastructure at all, only people who tell. Find an example of remembrance without a place and without an institution.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Choose a memory that matters to you. Decide where, how often and by whom it is to be recalled over the course of a year. Write this small infrastructure down in three lines.

sol-lewitt__claude-shannon.einstieg: Sol LeWitt's instructions can be transmitted like messages. Claude Shannon asks how information passes through a channel, regardless of what it means. A brief instruction can suffice to bring forth very complex works in different places. Yet between transmitted information and visible work lie decisions, material and execution. The instruction stays stable while its embodiment changes.

auftraege.beispiel: Name a very short instruction that brings forth something large: a rule of a game, a recipe, a set of directions. What has to be added for it to work?
auftraege.einwand: If so much comes into being during execution, perhaps the work does not lie in the instruction at all. Find an argument that information alone is not a work.
auftraege.gestaltung: Dictate a drawing to each other in no more than twenty words, without the person drawing being allowed to ask questions. Compare the idea and the result: which information was missing?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a very short instruction that brings forth something large: a rule of a game, a recipe, a set of directions. What has to be added for it to work?
auftraege_allein.einwand: If so much comes into being during execution, perhaps the work does not lie in the instruction at all. Find an argument that information alone is not a work.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write a drawing instruction in no more than twenty words. Put it aside for a while, then read it and draw only what it says. Compare the idea and the result: which information was missing?

donald-judd__jacques-derrida.einstieg: Donald Judd separates bodies by precise intervals and makes the space between them an essential part of the work. Jacques Derrida does not think distance only spatially. For him, identity also arises from the fact that something differs from other things and does not fully coincide with itself. Judd's intervals give this abstract difference a concrete spatial form.

auftraege.beispiel: Name two identical things that only become distinguishable through their distance: two windows, two chairs, two letters. What changes when the distance gets smaller?
auftraege.einwand: A thing is what it is, even all alone in empty space. Find an argument that identity does not depend on the distance to other things.
auftraege.gestaltung: Place three identical objects in a row. Change only the distances between them, twice. Each time, describe in one sentence what the row is now.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name two identical things that only become distinguishable through their distance: two windows, two chairs, two letters. What changes when the distance gets smaller?
auftraege_allein.einwand: A thing is what it is, even all alone in empty space. Find an argument that identity does not depend on the distance to other things.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Place three identical objects in a row. Change only the distances between them, twice. Each time, describe in one sentence what the row is now.

eva-hesse__henri-bergson.einstieg: Eva Hesse's materials age, sag, discolour and change their tension. One could record that as a sequence of separate states. Henri Bergson warns against laying time side by side like that. Duration means: what is past goes on working in the now. Hesse's material makes this almost physically visible. Today's latex does not replace yesterday's; its form has emerged from its whole history.

auftraege.beispiel: Look together at an object that has lived with you for a long time: a bag, a wooden spoon, a book. What trace of its history do you discover that makes it beautiful right now?
auftraege.einwand: Sometimes we wish for things that do not age. Find a case, between you, in which it is good that something stays unchanged.
auftraege.gestaltung: Take a sheet of paper and fold it together five times, each time a little differently. Then smooth it flat. Tell each other what the folds now reveal about its time.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Look at an object that has lived with you for a long time: a bag, a wooden spoon, a book. What trace of its history do you discover that makes it beautiful right now?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Sometimes we wish for things that do not age. Find a case in which it is good that something stays unchanged.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Take a sheet of paper and fold it five times, each time a little differently. Then smooth it flat. What do the folds now tell you about its time?

tehching-hsieh__donna-haraway.einstieg: Tehching Hsieh's time rules seem entirely general: an hour has sixty minutes for everyone. Donna Haraway reminds us that every experience is bound to a place and a body. For Hsieh's body, the same hour means something different depending on sleep, tiredness and weather. The clock establishes equality; the body experiences difference.

auftraege.beispiel: Tell each other about an hour that passed for you quite differently from what the clock said. What stretched or compressed your time like that?
auftraege.einwand: The same time for everyone can also protect: in working hours, in breaks, in deadlines. Look together for an argument that the clock can be fair.
auftraege.gestaltung: Set an alarm for five minutes. In that time, each of you do something completely different. Afterwards, describe how long your five minutes were.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of an hour that passed for you quite differently from what the clock said. What stretched or compressed your time like that?
auftraege_allein.einwand: The same time for everyone can also protect: in working hours, in breaks, in deadlines. Look for an argument that the clock can be fair.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Set an alarm for five minutes and in that time do something that does you good. Afterwards, describe how long your five minutes felt.

dan-graham__elena-esposito.einstieg: Dan Graham's time-delayed video shows the present only once it has already passed. What appears on the monitor is what you did just a moment ago. And while this image appears, you are already waiting for the next one. Elena Esposito examines how the future acts in the present even though it is not yet there. In Graham's work, the future arises precisely through the delay.

auftraege.beispiel: When did you last wait for something that was already on its way: an answer, a parcel, a person? How did the waiting change your moment?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps delay also takes something from us: spontaneity, closeness, the now. Find a case in which immediacy is more precious than expectation.
auftraege.gestaltung: One of you slowly makes a gesture; the other repeats it three seconds later. Swap roles. Tell each other what it feels like to watch your own doing from a moment behind.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: When did you last wait for something that was already on its way: an answer, a parcel, a person? How did the waiting change your moment?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps delay also takes something from us: spontaneity, closeness, the now. Find a case in which immediacy is more precious than expectation.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Film yourself for ten seconds making a calm movement and watch the recording straight afterwards. What do you notice when you watch your own doing from a moment behind?

felix-gonzalez-torres__hannah-arendt.einstieg: Hannah Arendt links the common world to things that endure between people. Felix Gonzalez-Torres makes works whose parts precisely do not need to be permanent. Sweets are eaten, sheets taken away and later replaced. Still, a work remains that different people can relate to at different times. The permanence lies not in the single thing but in a form that is maintained together.

auftraege.beispiel: Name something that exists only because many people keep renewing it: a festival, a garden, a song. What contribution have you yourselves already made to it?
auftraege.einwand: Some shared things need precisely a fixed, lasting object: a house, a monument, a book. Find an argument for the power of the permanent.
auftraege.gestaltung: Together, set out something small that others may take with them: a note with a good sentence, a flower, a nut. How does it feel that it travels on?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name something that exists only because many people keep renewing it: a festival, a garden, a song. What contribution have you yourself already made to it?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some shared things need precisely a fixed, lasting object: a house, a monument, a book. Find an argument for the power of the permanent.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Set out something small that others may take with them: a note with a good sentence, a flower, a nut. How does it feel that it travels on?

rebecca-horn__judith-butler.einstieg: Rebecca Horn alters bodies with extensions, masks and mechanical additions. Judith Butler asks how social norms determine which bodies are taken for granted and how they are read. Horn's apparatuses disturb that self-evidence. They show a body whose limits and possibilities are not fixed, without its becoming arbitrary.

auftraege.beispiel: Where does your body end, for you: at the skin, at your clothes, at the edge of your shadow? Tell each other about a moment when that boundary shifted.
auftraege.einwand: Clear bodily boundaries can also give support and protection. Look for an example in which a firm boundary is good and important.
auftraege.gestaltung: Make a small extension for a hand out of paper, string or cardboard. Try together to touch something or pass something with it. What more can your body suddenly do?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Where does your body end, for you: at the skin, at your clothes, at the edge of your shadow? Remember a moment when that boundary shifted.
auftraege_allein.einwand: Clear bodily boundaries can also give support and protection. Look for an example in which a firm boundary is good and important.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Make a small extension for your hand out of paper, string or cardboard. Touch something with it or pass something on. What more can your body suddenly do?

marina-abramovic__jacques-derrida.einstieg: Marina Abramović ties performance to the presence of a body in a present that cannot be repeated. Jacques Derrida shows that an event can only be passed on if traces of it become repeatable. Photographs, descriptions and videos do not rescue the original presence. They create new situations in which the past returns differently.

auftraege.beispiel: Tell each other about a moment you would have liked to hold on to, and how you still carry it within you today. What of it can be passed on?
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps a photograph does preserve more than we think. Find an example in which a recording saved something essential.
auftraege.gestaltung: Give each other a minute of undivided attention, without phone, without words. Afterwards, describe in one sentence what of it should remain.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a moment you would have liked to hold on to, and how you still carry it within you today. What of it could be passed on?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps a photograph does preserve more than we think. Find an example in which a recording saved something essential.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Give the room you are in a minute of undivided attention, without your phone. Afterwards, describe in one sentence what of it should remain.

mona-hatoum__lucy-suchman.einstieg: Mona Hatoum's rooms often feel familiar until a small shift changes how one moves through them. Lucy Suchman shows that action does not simply follow a plan but takes shape in the situation. A floor plan can fix where things stand. How a body finds its way among them, hesitates or steps aside is decided only on the spot.

auftraege.beispiel: Think of a room you often walk through. Where do you slow down, where do you step aside, where do you like to stop? What guided you there?
auftraege.einwand: Good plans make rooms easier to move through for many people. Look together for an argument that a room can be thought out in advance.
auftraege.gestaltung: Together, move a chair or a bag by an arm's length. Then both walk through the room and watch what your paths make of it.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a room you often walk through. Where do you slow down, where do you step aside, where do you like to stop? What guided you there?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Good plans make rooms easier to move through for many people. Look for an argument that a room can be thought out in advance.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Move a chair or a bag by an arm's length. Then walk through the room and watch what your path makes of it.

louise-bourgeois__claude-shannon.einstieg: Louise Bourgeois translates biographical experience again and again into rooms, bodies and recurring motifs. Claude Shannon can describe how signs are transmitted reliably, but not what personal meaning they carry. In Bourgeois's work this limit becomes fruitful. A spider, a house or a part of a body can be passed on without the memory from which the form arose going with it.

auftraege.beispiel: Show each other an object that a memory is attached to. What does the other person see, and what stays with you alone?
auftraege.einwand: Sometimes a memory does arrive: in a letter, a recipe, a song. Find an example in which transmission succeeded surprisingly well.
auftraege.gestaltung: Each of you draw a simple shape that carries a memory for you. Swap the drawings and tell each other what you see in the other person's shape.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Pick up an object that a memory is attached to. What would a stranger see in it, and what stays with you alone?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Sometimes a memory does arrive: in a letter, a recipe, a song. Find an example in which transmission succeeded surprisingly well.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Draw a simple shape that carries a memory for you. Write underneath what another person might see in it, and what only you see in it.

on-kawara__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.einstieg: On Kawara ties each date painting to a single day and a strict rule. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun studies digital media that create the impression of a continuing present through constant updating. In Kawara's work, each day is closed off and becomes irretrievably past. In the digital update, the past is continually overwritten so that something can appear present.

auftraege.beispiel: Scroll back together in your minds: which message, which picture from last week have you already almost forgotten? What would you like to keep?
auftraege.einwand: Updates keep many things alive: maps, timetables, news. Find an argument that overwriting can also be a form of care.
auftraege.gestaltung: Each of you write on a sheet of paper what was important to you today, and date it. Put it somewhere no one will overwrite it.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Scroll back in your mind: which message, which picture from last week have you already almost forgotten? What would you like to keep?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Updates keep many things alive: maps, timetables, news. Find an argument that overwriting can also be a form of care.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write on a sheet of paper what was important to you today, and date it. Put it somewhere no one will overwrite it.

doris-salcedo__michel-serres.einstieg: Doris Salcedo makes absent people present through furniture, fabrics, cracks and other material traces, without replacing them. Michel Serres is interested in mediators and passages that change what they carry. In this sense Salcedo's material is no neutral messenger. It carries the loss onward by giving it a new form, a different weight and a new place.

auftraege.beispiel: Is there an object in your home that reminds you of a person who is no longer there or lives far away? Tell each other how it carries that absence.
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps memory needs no material at all, only a conversation. Find an example in which words are enough.
auftraege.gestaltung: Together, choose a small object and give it a task for this evening: to remind you of someone. Where do you put it?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Is there an object in your home that reminds you of a person who is no longer there or lives far away? Feel how it carries that absence.
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps memory needs no material at all, only a conversation. Find an example in which words are enough.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Choose a small object and give it a task for this evening: to remind you of someone. Where do you put it?

sol-lewitt__susan-leigh-star.einstieg: Sol LeWitt's instructions allow a work to be carried out in different places without his own hand. Susan Leigh Star draws attention to the infrastructures that make something like that seem self-evident. The people executing it, prepared walls, documentation, material and knowledge form a net without which the rule does not become a work. The idea seems free because its infrastructure works reliably.

auftraege.beispiel: Think of an idea of your own that became real. Who or what helped in the background without anyone noticing? Thank those helpers in your thoughts.
auftraege.einwand: Sometimes an idea needs only one person and a sheet of paper. Find an example of an idea that managed almost without infrastructure.
auftraege.gestaltung: Write down a small idea you would both like to carry out this week. Next to it, note three things that will support it. Which of them do you already have?

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of an idea of your own that became real. Who or what helped in the background without anyone noticing? Thank those helpers in your thoughts.
auftraege_allein.einwand: Sometimes an idea needs only one person and a sheet of paper. Find an example of an idea that managed almost without infrastructure.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write down a small idea you would like to carry out this week. Next to it, note three things that will support it. Which of them do you already have?

donald-judd__george-spencer-brown.einstieg: George Spencer-Brown begins with a distinction that separates two sides from each other. Donald Judd's works show that the distance between things can perform such a separation too. The space between is not simply empty. It holds bodies apart, determines their relationship and lets a sequence of individual forms arise. Without distance, the elements would collapse into a different form.

auftraege.beispiel: Where does a distance do something good in your lives: between cups on a shelf, between words, between two people? Tell each other a favourite example.
auftraege.einwand: Some things only become beautiful when they touch: hands, colours, voices. Find an argument for moving closer together.
auftraege.gestaltung: Lay five small things in a row, first close together, then with wide gaps. Together, look for the distance at which the row seems most alive to you.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Where does a distance do something good in your life: between cups on a shelf, between words, between two people? Name your favourite example.
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some things only become beautiful when they touch: hands, colours, voices. Find an argument for moving closer together.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Lay five small things in a row, first close together, then with wide gaps. Look for the distance at which the row seems most alive to you.

donald-judd__susan-leigh-star.einstieg: Donald Judd's works often appear as self-contained, precisely placed bodies. Susan Leigh Star turns our attention to infrastructures that make stability possible in the background. Judd's precision too depends on less visible conditions: fabrication, measurements, wall, floor, fixings. The distance between two elements is therefore no empty space. It has to be produced anew at every presentation.

auftraege.beispiel: What keeps something exactly in its place in your home: a nail, a habit, a practised hand movement? Tell each other who sees to it.
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps precision is sometimes not needed at all, and roughly is quite enough. Find an example in which imprecision does good.
auftraege.gestaltung: Place two cups exactly a hand's breadth apart. Check in an hour whether the distance is still right, and tell each other what has kept or changed it.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: What keeps something exactly in its place in your home: a nail, a habit, a practised hand movement? Who sees to it?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps precision is sometimes not needed at all, and roughly is quite enough. Find an example in which imprecision does good.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Place two cups exactly a hand's breadth apart. Check in an hour whether the distance is still right, and note down what has kept or changed it.

on-kawara__henri-bergson.einstieg: On Kawara's date paintings give a day an unambiguous place in the calendar. Henri Bergson distinguishes such measurable time from lived duration, which does not consist of equal units. Kawara's rule brings the two together in a single picture. The day is precisely named and closed, while the work on it is experienced as tiredness, rhythm and attention.

auftraege.beispiel: Name a date that is full of duration for you: a birthday, a move, a first day at school. What all fits into that one day?
auftraege.einwand: Calendars help us arrange to meet and find one another. Find an argument for the power of the clear number.
auftraege.gestaltung: Write today's date slowly and beautifully, each digit with care. Tell each other what went through your minds while you were writing.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Name a date that is full of duration for you: a birthday, a move, a first day at school. What all fits into that one day?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Calendars help people arrange to meet and find each other again. Find an argument for the power of the clear number.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write today's date slowly and beautifully, each digit with care. Then note down what went through your mind while you were writing.

tehching-hsieh__michel-serres.einstieg: Tehching Hsieh designs rules meant to hold over a long time with as few exceptions as possible. Michel Serres is interested in disturbance, and in the fact that a channel often becomes visible precisely through its interruptions. In Hsieh's work, sleep, tiredness, illness and everyday life constantly threaten the pure going on. The possible disturbance therefore belongs to the performance, even if it is meant to be avoided.

auftraege.beispiel: Remember a habit that you only noticed when it once failed to happen. What did you discover about yourselves in that moment?
auftraege.einwand: Some rules work best when nobody notices them. Find an example in which an invisible rule carries you.
auftraege.gestaltung: Interrupt a small routine for three minutes: sit differently, hold the cup in the other hand. Tell each other what the disturbance made visible.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Remember a habit that you only noticed when it once failed to happen. What did you discover about yourself in that moment?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some rules work best when nobody notices them. Find an example in which an invisible rule carries you.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Interrupt a small routine for three minutes: sit differently, hold the cup in the other hand. What did the disturbance make visible to you?

dan-graham__lucy-suchman.einstieg: Dan Graham plans reflections, glass surfaces and video delays very precisely. Lucy Suchman shows, however, that an arrangement does not determine how people actually behave within it. In Graham's work, the piece therefore also arises from reactions, glances and movements that appear in no plan beforehand. The construction is precise; the situation remains open.

auftraege.beispiel: Tell each other about a plan from which something came that was more beautiful than planned. What happened in between?
auftraege.einwand: A good plan can give security and make freedom possible in the first place. Find an example in which the plan was the most important thing.
auftraege.gestaltung: Together, plan a two-minute walk through the room, step by step. Then walk it and notice what turned out differently along the way.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a plan from which something came that was more beautiful than planned. What happened in between?
auftraege_allein.einwand: A good plan can give security and make freedom possible in the first place. Find an example in which the plan was the most important thing.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Plan a two-minute walk through the room, step by step. Then walk it and notice what turned out differently along the way.

marina-abramovic__hannah-arendt.einstieg: Marina Abramović makes presence before others part of her performances. Hannah Arendt describes a space of appearance that arises where people become visible to one another and act before one another. For Abramović, the public is therefore not just an audience in the background. The presence of others changes the situation in which a body appears.

auftraege.beispiel: When did you last feel that simply being there had an effect, without a word? Tell each other about it.
auftraege.einwand: Sometimes it takes precisely the unobserved to be free. Find an example in which being alone is more valuable than being in public.
auftraege.gestaltung: Sit quietly facing each other for a minute and simply be there. Afterwards, describe what that presence did to you.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: When did you last feel that simply being there had an effect, without a word? Recall it.
auftraege_allein.einwand: Sometimes it takes precisely the unobserved to be free. Find an example in which being alone is more valuable than being in public.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Sit for a minute at a window or among people and simply be there. Afterwards, describe what that presence did to you.

mona-hatoum__george-spencer-brown.einstieg: George Spencer-Brown begins with the drawing of a boundary through which two sides come into being. Mona Hatoum makes such separations physically uncertain. A grille can mean protection or captivity, a threshold access or exclusion. Which side is inside or outside depends not only on the line but also on where the body stands. The boundary stays simple; its meaning does not.

auftraege.beispiel: Think of a door, a fence or a threshold in your lives. When was it protection, when an obstacle? Tell each other what changed.
auftraege.einwand: Some boundaries give shelter and calm. Look for an example in which a clear side is good for everyone.
auftraege.gestaltung: Lay a piece of string on the floor as a line. Stand on different sides and describe what you see from there. Then swap places.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a door, a fence or a threshold in your life. When was it protection, when an obstacle? What changed?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some boundaries give shelter and calm. Look for an example in which a clear side is good for everyone.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Lay a piece of string on the floor as a line. Stand on one side, then on the other, and describe what you see from each.

louise-bourgeois__donna-haraway.einstieg: Louise Bourgeois makes memory spatial without smoothing it into a general story. Donna Haraway wishes for a knowledge that knows its own standpoint. In Bourgeois's Cells, things therefore do not appear as neutral evidence of a past. They are bound to body, biography, place and line of sight, and yet remain accessible to others.

auftraege.beispiel: Tell each other a small memory from your childhood, with a detail only you know: a smell, a colour, a sound. What of it can the other person feel with you?
auftraege.einwand: Some memories may remain entirely private, and that is a good thing. Find an argument for not making everything legible.
auftraege.gestaltung: Each choose an object that carries a memory and place it so that it tells its story from your line of sight. Explain to each other why just so.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a small memory from your childhood, with a detail only you know: a smell, a colour, a sound. How might another person feel it with you?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Some memories may remain entirely private, and that is a good thing. Find an argument for not making everything legible.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Choose an object that carries a memory and place it so that it tells its story from your line of sight. Describe why just so.

doris-salcedo__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.einstieg: Doris Salcedo creates material traces that do not need to appear anew through constant updating. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun, by contrast, describes digital presence as something that persists through repetition and update. Salcedo's works set a slower form of duration against this. Their materials remain and change without passing themselves off as new.

auftraege.beispiel: Which memory do you keep renewing, and which simply rests quietly with you? Tell each other about both.
auftraege.einwand: Perhaps memory stays alive precisely through renewal: in telling, in celebrating, in sharing. Find an example of this.
auftraege.gestaltung: Each of you find an object that was allowed to grow old without being renewed. Lay it between you and describe what it knows about staying.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Which memory do you keep renewing, and which simply rests quietly with you? Think of both.
auftraege_allein.einwand: Perhaps memory stays alive precisely through renewal: in telling, in celebrating, in sharing. Find an example of this.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Find an object that was allowed to grow old without being renewed. Lay it in front of you and describe what it knows about staying.

sol-lewitt__jacques-derrida.einstieg: Sol LeWitt's instructions can be carried out again in different places and at different times. Jacques Derrida calls this repeatability iterability. A sign must be able to detach itself from its context in order to be repeatable, and precisely through this its context changes. LeWitt's rule remains recognisable, and every repetition exposes it to other spatial and material conditions.

auftraege.beispiel: Do you have a favourite recipe or a ritual that you always do the same way and that still turns out a little different each time? Tell each other what changes.
auftraege.einwand: Sometimes repetition succeeds astonishingly exactly: in print, in music, in craft. Find an argument for the identical copy.
auftraege.gestaltung: Each of you write the same short sentence three times by hand. Lay the six lines side by side and discover together where each repetition became its own.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Do you have a favourite recipe or a ritual that you always do the same way and that still turns out a little different each time? What changes?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Sometimes repetition succeeds astonishingly exactly: in print, in music, in craft. Find an argument for the identical copy.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Write the same short sentence three times by hand. Lay the lines side by side and discover where each repetition became its own.

rebecca-horn__elena-esposito.einstieg: Elena Esposito stresses that forecasts do not know the future but generate expectations in the present. Rebecca Horn's machines seem to fix a sequence in advance. Yet as soon as mechanics meets body, friction and space, the intended sequence becomes an actual event. The machine makes the future more calculable without already turning it into present.

auftraege.beispiel: Think of a device you trust to work again tomorrow. Where does that trust come from, and has it ever surprised you?
auftraege.einwand: Calculability can relieve us and make room for the unexpected. Find an example in which a good prediction gives freedom.
auftraege.gestaltung: Let an object roll across the table three times, and each predict beforehand where it will come to rest. Enjoy every deviation.

auftraege_allein.beispiel: Think of a device you trust to work again tomorrow. Where does that trust come from, and has it ever surprised you?
auftraege_allein.einwand: Calculability can relieve us and make room for the unexpected. Find an example in which a good prediction gives freedom.
auftraege_allein.gestaltung: Let an object roll across the table three times and predict beforehand where it will come to rest. Enjoy every deviation.

eva-hesse__judith-butler.einstieg: Eva Hesse repeats forms without producing identical bodies. Judith Butler understands repetition as an enactment through which an order persists and can at the same time change. In Hesse's work this change becomes visible in the material. Each execution belongs to the series and yet remains a body of its own. Sameness and singularity do not exclude each other here.

auftraege.beispiel: Think of a set of things that belong together and yet are all different: cups, siblings, the trees of an avenue. What makes each single one dear to you?
auftraege.einwand: Sometimes sameness is exactly what matters, with screws, say, or medicines or rules. Find an argument for the identical.
auftraege.gestaltung: Each of you form five small identical balls from paper, modelling clay or bread dough. Lay them side by side and tell each other which one touches you most, and why.

felix-gonzalez-torres__claude-shannon.einstieg: Felix Gonzalez-Torres can describe a work through certificate, measurements and rules so that it can be installed afresh in different places. Claude Shannon shows how information can be transmitted reliably, independently of its meaning. Yet the complete specifications do not yet produce the same situation. Weight, taking away, audience and replenishment have to happen first.

auftraege.beispiel: Name something that was described to you precisely and turned out quite different in reality: a place, a dish, a person. What was in no description?
auftraege.einwand: Good instructions make many things possible, from furniture to songs. Find an example in which a description passes on almost everything.
auftraege.gestaltung: Describe to each other, in three sentences, a place you love, as precisely as you can. Then ask: what is still missing for the other person to really be there?
